title: From Hospital to Assisted Living in Memphis: The Discharge Timeline and What to Have Ready in 72 Hours
description: Moving a parent from a Memphis hospital to assisted living: the discharge timeline, who the discharge planner is, your Medicare rights, and what to have ready in 72 hours.
meta_title: Hospital to Assisted Living in Memphis: Discharge Guide
meta_description: Moving a parent from a Memphis hospital to assisted living: the discharge timeline, the discharge planner, your Medicare rights, and a 72-hour checklist.
main_html:
Quick answer

When a parent in a Memphis hospital cannot safely go home, tell the hospital's discharge planner or case manager on the first day that you are looking at assisted living. Ask for the planned discharge date and the level of care they recommend. Then contact two or three licensed communities near the hospital or near family. Every community will need the discharge summary, a current medication list, physician orders and a TB screening before it can accept your parent. With those ready, many communities can assess and admit within a few days of an opening.

A hospital discharge plan is the hospital's written plan for where a patient goes next and what care they need there. A discharge planner or case manager, usually a nurse or social worker, prepares it with the patient and family, arranges referrals, and sends the records the next setting needs to accept the patient.

Hospitals move quickly. Discharge can be planned within a day or two of admission, and families who wait for the hospital to suggest a plan often find the only options offered are going home or a nursing home with a bed that day.

The discharge timeline

  1. Day 1, admission: ask who the case manager or discharge planner is and how to reach them. Tell them your parent lives alone, or is not safe at home, and that you want to look at assisted living. Ask whether your parent is an inpatient or under observation.
  2. Day 1 to 2: the hospital assesses your parent's needs; therapists may evaluate walking and transfers. Ask what level of care they recommend: home, home with home health, short-term rehab in a skilled nursing facility, or assisted living.
  3. Day 2 to 3: call communities. Ask whether they have an opening of the right type, whether they can assess in the hospital, and what paperwork they need.
  4. Day 3 to 4: a community nurse assesses your parent, in person or from records. The hospital sends the discharge summary, medication list and orders.
  5. Discharge day: transport arranged, medications either sent with your parent or ordered to the community's pharmacy, family at the community to help settle.

When your parent needs rehab first, the order changes: hospital, then a skilled nursing facility for therapy, then assisted living. That gives you more time to choose a community, so use it.

Who the discharge planner is

Every hospital has staff whose job is to plan safe discharges. They may be called case managers, care coordinators or social workers. In large Memphis hospitals such as Baptist Memorial Hospital-Memphis, Methodist University Hospital, Saint Francis Hospital-Park Avenue and Regional One Health, each unit usually has an assigned case manager. They:

  • Assess what care your parent will need after discharge.
  • Arrange referrals to skilled nursing facilities, home health agencies and, where the family asks, assisted living communities.
  • Send the records the next setting needs.
  • Explain what insurance will and will not pay for.

They are busy, and they are working to the hospital's timetable. Be clear and early about your plan, and ask them to send records to the communities you choose.

What to have ready in 72 hours

  • Discharge summary: diagnoses, what happened in hospital, and the plan.
  • Medication list: every medicine with dose and timing, including changes made in hospital.
  • Physician orders: diet, activity, therapy, wound care, and a statement that your parent's needs can be met in assisted living. Communities may have their own physician form.
  • TB screening: a recent test or chest X-ray result. Ask the hospital to do or record it if it is not on file.
  • Therapy notes: walking, transfers and equipment needs.
  • Insurance cards and Medicare number, and any long-term care policy.
  • Power of attorney and advance directives, if they exist.
  • A one-page description of your parent's normal day, likes and routines.
  • Equipment: walker, wheelchair or shower chair ordered if needed.

Your Medicare rights at discharge

If your parent has Medicare and is a hospital inpatient, the hospital must give them the notice called An Important Message from Medicare About Your Rights, near admission and again before discharge. It explains the right to appeal a discharge you think is too early, through the Quality Improvement Organization named on the notice. Follow the notice's instructions and deadline; if you appeal in time, your parent can usually stay while the appeal is decided.

Two Medicare facts that change plans:

  • Inpatient or observation: Medicare covers a skilled nursing facility stay only after a qualifying inpatient stay of at least three days. Time under observation does not count, even if your parent was in a hospital bed. Ask early which status your parent has.
  • Assisted living is not covered: Medicare does not pay for assisted living. If your parent goes from hospital to assisted living, the family pays from the first day, though Medicare can still cover home health visits, therapy and doctors there.

Communities near each Memphis hospital

Families often look near the hospital that treats their parent, so follow-up appointments are close. These pages list the nearest licensed communities, with phone numbers, licence numbers and memory care:

What to ask communities when time is short

  1. Do you have an opening in the type of apartment we need, now or within the week?
  2. Can your nurse assess my parent in the hospital, or from records?
  3. Which forms do you need from the hospital and the doctor?
  4. Can you meet these needs: [read the key items from the discharge summary]?
  5. What is the all-in monthly price at the likely care level?
  6. How are medications handled on the day of arrival?

Cross off any community that cannot answer the first four.

If no community can take your parent in time

Sometimes the hospital is ready to discharge before a community can admit. Options:

  • Short-term rehab: if your parent qualifies, a skilled nursing stay gives time to recover and choose.
  • Respite stay: some assisted living communities offer short furnished respite stays, which can turn into a permanent move.
  • Home with help: home health and private aides for a short period, with family staying.
  • Appeal: if you believe the discharge is unsafe, use the Medicare appeal on the Important Message notice.

Do not accept a discharge home that you believe is unsafe without saying so clearly to the case manager and the doctor, in writing if needed.

Move-in day

  • Confirm the time with the community and the transport.
  • Make sure medications arrive with your parent or are delivered the same day; ask who checks them against the hospital list.
  • Bring clothes for a week, toiletries, glasses, hearing aids, dentures and chargers.
  • Set up a few familiar things in the apartment before your parent arrives.
  • Meet the nurse or wellness director and agree when you will next talk.

The first weeks after a hospital stay are when falls and medication errors are most likely. Visit often, and ask the community how it is monitoring your parent.

Paying when it happens fast

A sudden move leaves little time to plan money. Ask the community about the first month's payment and the community fee, and whether any can be deferred while a house sale, an insurance claim or a VA application is under way. Our guide on how families pay covers short-term options including bridge loans.

Questions to ask the hospital

  • Who is the case manager, and how do I reach them?
  • Is my parent an inpatient or under observation?
  • What discharge date are you planning?
  • What level of care do you recommend, and why?
  • Will you send the discharge summary, medication list and orders to the communities we name?
  • Has a TB screening been done or can it be done before discharge?
  • What equipment will my parent need, and who orders it?

When rehab comes first

After a fall, a fracture, a stroke or a serious illness, the hospital often recommends short-term rehabilitation in a skilled nursing facility before any move to assisted living. If your parent was an inpatient for at least three days and needs daily skilled therapy or nursing, Medicare can cover the stay, in full for the first 20 days and with a daily coinsurance after that, for up to 100 days in a benefit period.

Use the rehab weeks well. Tour assisted living communities, have the rehab facility's therapists describe your parent's progress to the community's nurse, and line up an apartment for the day rehab ends. The rehab facility has its own discharge planner who can help with the next move.

Medications on the day of the move

Medication errors are among the most common problems after a hospital discharge. Ask the hospital for a reconciled medication list that says which medicines are new, which were stopped and which doses changed. Give that list to the community, and ask which pharmacy will fill prescriptions and when the first delivery will arrive. If there is any gap, ask the hospital whether it can supply the first doses, or arrange to pick them up yourself.

If you live away from Memphis

Many adult children manage a parent's hospital discharge from another city. Tell the case manager on day one that you are out of town and agree how you will be contacted, ideally a daily call at a set time. Ask the hospital to add you to your parent's authorised contacts so staff can speak to you. Have the power of attorney and HIPAA authorisation scanned and ready to email.

Ask communities whether their nurse can assess your parent in the hospital and talk to you by phone, and whether they will do a live video tour. If a friend, neighbour or church member in Memphis can visit the shortlisted communities with the tour checklist, use them. Plan to be in Memphis for move-in day and the first few days after; that is when your presence helps most.

faq.q: Can a parent go straight from hospital to assisted living?
faq.a: Yes, if their needs can be met in assisted living and a community has an opening. The community will need the discharge summary, medication list, physician orders and a TB screening, and will assess your parent first.

faq.q: Who arranges the move from hospital to assisted living?
faq.a: The hospital's discharge planner or case manager coordinates the discharge and sends records. The family usually chooses the community and arranges the move, with the case manager's help.

faq.q: How fast can assisted living admit a parent from hospital?
faq.a: Often within a few days of an opening, once the community has assessed your parent and has the paperwork. Having the documents ready is what usually makes it quick.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for assisted living after a hospital stay?
faq.a: No. Medicare can pay for a short skilled nursing stay after a qualifying inpatient stay of at least three days, but not for assisted living. It still covers doctors, therapy and home health visits there.

faq.q: What is observation status and why does it matter?
faq.a: A patient under observation is technically an outpatient even if in a hospital bed. Observation days do not count toward the three-day inpatient stay Medicare requires before it covers skilled nursing.

faq.q: Can we appeal a hospital discharge?
faq.a: Yes. Medicare patients receive An Important Message from Medicare About Your Rights, which explains how to appeal to the Quality Improvement Organization named on it. Follow the deadline on the notice.

faq.q: What if no assisted living community can take my parent in time?
faq.a: Ask about short-term rehab if your parent qualifies, a respite stay at a community, or home with temporary help. If you believe a discharge home is unsafe, say so in writing and consider an appeal.

faq.q: Which communities are near the big Memphis hospitals?
faq.a: This site has pages listing the licensed communities nearest Baptist Memorial Hospital-Memphis, Methodist University Hospital, Saint Francis Hospital-Park Avenue and Regional One Health, with phone and licence numbers.
